Stress in polysyllabic nominal roots [heading]. Stress in trisyllabic unreduplicated nominal roots is predominantly on the penultimate syllable, expecially [sic] if this syllable is closed. However, there are many ... trisyllabic roots in which word stress is on the first syllable, and a few in which stress may variably occur on the first or the penultimate syllable. Those in which stress usually occurs on the first syllable generally have open penultimate syllable, but exceptions to this are found. Examples of the two patterns, first and penultimate syllable stress, are: ... waláyjnin 'shade, shadow' ... wánulu 'good-for-nothing' ... new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog's weight-sensitive tier record (Merlan 1982 'Penultimate stress norm', 3.3.2.4, with many initial-stressed trisyllabic roots). The chapter frames the initial-stressed words as lexical exceptions to a penultimate system; the catalog's E-record formalises Merlan's open-penult tendency as a categorical weight rule (weight-sensitive (tentative), second reader V: rule INCONSISTENT at 9/6). Those are two framings of the same data, not a contradiction; the chapter adds nothing about syllable weight in the reachable text. The listed open_url is the WRONG ITEM (Grant ch. 30) and should be dropped from the open-copy list; second-attempt downloads (Leiden repository, van…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The chapter classes Mangarayi (with Ngalakan) as a penultimate-stress language that has 'scores' of lexical initial-stress exceptions; ex. (23) lists forms with primary stress on the first syllable and secondary on the penult (ˈwuruˌmumu) and forms with the reverse (ˌmiliˈbalkiñ, ˌwarinˈjalan). What 'Merlan notes' after the table is cut off by the snippet.
new_statements.secondary_stress: The (23) forms show a second, weaker stress two syllables away from the primary in four-syllable words (initial+penult), consistent with Merlan's 'primary and secondary stresses fall on penultimate and first syllables' for quadrisyllabic roots; no general secondary-stress rule is visible in the snippet.
new_statements.exceptions: Initial-stress exceptions to the penultimate norm, described as numerous ('scores'); the snippet does not say whether they are weight-conditioned.
new_statements.identity_note: Example (23) in the 2017 chapter is a two-column Ngalakan / Mangarayi table; the snippet flattens the columns, so which of ˈdakbaˌrara, ˈwuruˌmumu, ˌmiliˈbalkiñ, ˌwarinˈjalan are Mangarayi is not recoverable from it (wurumumu 'hornet' is independently Merlan's Mangarayi wúrumūmu; dakbarara is unassigned). The wrong-item PDF (Grant, Western Micronesian Sprachbund) concerns Chuukic, Yapese, Palauan and Chamorro, not any Australian language.

readall_conflicts: No contradiction between sources on placement: Merlan 1982 (catalog, snippets), Goedemans 2010 (carried in the catalog record) and the van der Hulst/Goedemans/Rice 2017 chapter all describe a penultimate norm with a sizeable set of initial-stressed words. They differ in how they treat those words: the 2017 chapter (and Goedemans 2010: 'clearly belong to a set of regular exceptions') calls them lexical exceptions, while the catalog's weight-sensitive tier E-record encodes Merlan's 'especially if closed' / 'generally have open penultimate syllable' hedge as a categorical closed-penult rule, which the tier's own second reader scored at 9 agree / 6 disagree. The hedged (weight-sensitive (tentative)) classification already records that tension.
